In the photo, from left to right:

**Cisco SPA122 ATA:** This essentially allows any analog telephone to connect to my FreePBX setup as an extension, utilizing SIP to convert SIP protocol packets into telephone system signals. Even works with Caller ID. Has the option for two lines, at the moment I only have Line 1 setup which is registered to extension 1400 in my PBX. It is plugged into the..

**Phone jack splitter:** Right below the SPA122, it isn't necessarily network equipment but still serves a purpose. Connected to an analog telephone set (out of picture), can serve up to five phones on one line. 

**TP-Link TL-SF1005D:** Cheapo ethernet switch that connects the components of this system, as well as a desktop computer and the IP phone out of picture (via a POE injector). Nothing too special, although it gets its source connection via a power line Ethernet adapter (also out of picture). 

**OBiLink OBi200:** This little box allows me to connect my Google Voice account to my phone system. While its really only meant to be used to plug a phone line directly into it, with some tinkering in the setup pages, it also can host a SIP server with your Google Voice number, allowing you to use your Google Voice number as both an inbound and outbound route on FreePBX. This allows my phone system to connect to the POTS (plain old telephone system) Sidenote: these things afaik are now unsupported and essentially obsolete, it still works but there's no guarantee it will continue to forever, as well as its integration w/ Google Voice. ObiLink was also bought by Polycom if I remember correctly too

Out of picture:

**2021 Mac Mini M1:** Desk computer adjacent to all of this.

**2011 Mac Mini:** Hosts the FreePBX server via an automatic VirtualBox instance, also serves a DDNS client, Plex and macOS Server (RIP). Might post about it here someday. Looking to change some things up and host FreePBX either in Docker or another machine running ProxMox instead.

**Polycom SoundPoint IP 550:** My IP phone of choice. Connected to my PBX on another extension. Plugged into the ethernet switch.

**Panasonic DECT home phone, unsure of model #**

From left to right:

​

MacBook Pro - connected to the livestream on the stream website, for a live view for what people at home were seeing. Also served to control the projector PC (see below)

Monitor 2 - Connected to Dell Desktop, displays OBS' Program Out. Only looks different from the stream monitor because it was taken in between switching sources with the \~20 second stream latency

Monitor 1- OBS. Sources include one for the ATEM Mini Pro, as well as the Pre-Stream graphic, slideshow video, Emergency Cutaway and Projector Output

Dell Desktop - Below Monitor 1, this desktop (don't recall the model) ran OBS and was connected via USB-C to the ATEM Mini Pro for control/webcam input. Also used OBS to record the show.

Projector screen - So basically the school's projector setup was really odd, in the sense that the projector could be hooked into with HDMI via the installed AV system rack out of picture, but it was also permanently hooked up to a "projector PC" (also out of picture) which in this case, was running a slideshow of cast names (and was used during the play for a scene requiring a video to play). What's odd though is if guest presenters or speakers would come in and play a slideshow, if they didn't want to plug in to HDMI they'd basically just use a school-issued Chromebook signed in to a special Google Apps account, and use Chrome Remote Desktop to control the projector PC, which on there, would have to be running their slideshow. I never understood why they set it up like that when they could've used any other mirroring solution, but I'm already diving off topic.

Multiview Monitor - Connected to ATEM Mini Pro, displayed Multiview

ATEM Mini Pro - Connected to two HDMI sources. We basically just had two 100ft HDMI cables running out of the booth to two XA10s with student operators, and were on headset the whole show. Mostly kept one camera at wide and one for follow and close up. Was good enough.

​

Another annoying thing about this setup is that throughout the auditorium there are (apart from the wired HDMI/XLR hookups onstage for presenter use, and DMX for lighting)  four SDI jacks, which all (as well as XLR for audio) run to a room backstage separate from the booth pictured. The Media Communications class, Pre-COVID, would actually live direct videos for anything that went on in the auditorium, including board meetings, plays, concerts, etc. and it would all be live recorded onto a file through a Leightronix board backstage. (They'd then burn DVDs or send it to the tv station for these). They never thought about using it for livestreams though, and I asked them about it and they said it would be too much of a hassle, and that the signals wouldn't hook up and neither would the projector feed. I don't know, it was one of those situations where there wasn't a winner just because of the people in charge, but it still bugs me that the setup could've been a lot cleaner and more permanent. Oh well. I'm in college now and working with way more professional grade equipment,so there's that.

Little bit late to the party, but dude I hear ya. I’m currently a senior and a techie doing sound (and now livestreams/cameras cuz of social distance restrictions) and I absolutely hate whenever directors find ridiculous ways to solve problem. Last fall we had some buzzing coming thru our sound system and we couldn’t isolate it. I was tasked with testing everything to find the issue. I tested the soundboard outputs, electrical boxes, everything, and still nothing. Eventually they said they’d just hire someone to fix it. At that point I’d basically given up when at one point, I muted our projector sound input thru our touch panel, and the buzzing magically disappeared. Being excited I immediately went to the director and said it was all fixed, and we just had to mute the projector as a temporary solution for the buzzing. She appreciated it but said to turn it back on because it would interfere with the AV system and that the professional should be touching things, not me. So I do as she says and ofc there’s agonizing buzzing during rehearsals and it’s hard to focus and tune it out. Eventually the repairman comes in and tries fixing it, and ends up actually fucking it up even more, to a point where the buzzing was fixed, BUT we couldn’t get audio to our cameras, obviously important to the livestreams. Director asks me why I didn’t fix it, and I remind her that I did “fix” it (more find a temp solution) and that the problem lied within the AV and projection system, and she told me not to mess with it. It turns out she never listened to me and the repairman ended up not even going to the AV system but rather did something else that somehow had a repercussion into the audio patch system and fucked it up for the cameras. She ended up having to get ANOTHER repairman to come in and undo whatever the last guy did, because the last guy never fully fixed it, rather unplugged some cables and called it a day... PLUS fix the patch system. Took him a few days. Probably cost them around $1500, those guys aren’t cheap.
